meaning.evidence: Every rule survives: separate eskies for drinks and perishables, "open the esky as little as you can", wrap raw meat, rinse produce, the jug-and-soap fallback, marinate in the fridge and "set a bit aside separately", partial cooking, the thermometer, side of the grill, clean platter. "platter or tongs" narrows "utensils" slightly.

sense.evidence: Most terms fit ("Stick cold food in an esky", "Meat, chook and seafood", "kitchen bench", "stops it getting cooked to buggery"), but "gives the nasty bugs in your tucker a real chance to go off" strains (bugs don't "go off", food does), and "out in the bush too" narrows "outdoor settings".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Australian giving advice: "once you've rocked up", "copping a dose of food poisoning", "when everyone's opening and shutting the drinks esky to grab another one". "wrapped up good and tight" is more American.

register.evidence: Full level-4 voice, swearing at dad level: "bacteria breed like bloody rabbits", "cooked to buggery".

tone.evidence: Still practical safety guidance, though jokier in places: "all that warm-weather carry-on", "breed like bloody rabbits"; the rules themselves stay clear.

flow.evidence: Reads naturally: "Give fresh fruit and veg a rinse under the running tap before they go in the esky". The opening "a real chance to go off" is a muddled join.

variety.evidence: Ranges widely without leaning on one word: "barbie", "tucker", "esky", "chook", "lugging", "rocked up", "copping", "dead important", "tea towel".

essence.evidence: Still the same picnic food-safety guide, headings and order intact: "Pack and Transport Food Safely", "Follow Safe Grilling Tips".

problems.quote: gives the nasty bugs in your tucker a real chance to go off
problems.original: present opportunities for foodborne bacteria to thrive
problems.why: "Go off" means food spoiling or a party getting wild, not bacteria thriving; the image is muddled.
A park picnic isn't "the bush"; narrows the sense.
"Good and tight" reads more American than Australian.

A.summary: A lively, varied level-4 retelling that keeps every safety rule; one or two strained phrases.

meaning.evidence: All the rules kept: "packing the drinks in one esky and the tucker that goes off in another", "set some aside separately before you add the raw meat", "have a clean platter and utensils ready next to the barbie".

sense.evidence: Terms fit their contexts: "frozen ice bricks", "the tucker that goes off" for perishables, "check your mitts". "Barbecued tucker" and "the raw tucker's juices" strain where "food" is the plain word.

authenticity.evidence: Natural phrases ("once you've rocked up", "won't cop the warm air outside") are undercut by "tucker" substituted almost everywhere: "Keep cold tucker cold. Put cold tucker in an esky".

register.evidence: Steady Aussie, a little under level 4: the slang is mostly nouns ("tucker", "esky", "barbie", "mitts") with plain sentences around them. No swearing, within the limit.

tone.evidence: Keeps the friendly advisory tone of a safety leaflet: "This helps keep what's inside colder for longer."

flow.evidence: Readable and clear, though the repeated noun clunks: "spread to the cooked tucker. Instead, have a clean platter and utensils ready next to the barbie to serve your tucker."

variety.evidence: Leans heavily on one word: "tucker" appears in nearly every paragraph, e.g. "Marinate tucker in the fridge", "Cook tucker right through", "Keep \"ready\" tucker hot".

essence.evidence: The same food-safety guide, structure kept: "Quick Tips for Setting Up at the Picnic Spot".

problems.why: Representative of "tucker" replacing "food" throughout; an Australian would wince at the repetition.

problems.quote: Barbecued tucker can be kept hot
problems.original: Grilled food can be kept hot
problems.why: "Tucker" strains in a technical cooking instruction.

B.summary: Accurate and readable, but leans on "tucker" in almost every line, making it sound mechanical.

meaning.evidence: Effectively the original with nouns swapped, so all the rules survive: "limit the number of times the esky is opened as much as you can".

sense.evidence: Most swaps fit ("esky", "kitchen bench", "once you’ve fronted up"), but "Grilled tucker" and "the beverage esky" strain against their formal frames.

authenticity.evidence: Slang nouns dropped into untouched American text: "Organize esky contents. Consider packing beverages in one esky", "Marinate tucker in the refrigerator"; US spelling "Organize" left in.

register.evidence: Far lighter than level 4: sentences are the original's ("Partial cooking before grilling is only safe when the partially cooked tucker can go on the hot grill immediately") with word swaps.

tone.evidence: The original advisory tone is intact: "This helps to keep the contents cold longer."

flow.evidence: The swaps jar against formal prose and mix forms: "contaminating prepared/cooked tucker or foods that will be eaten raw", "Keep “ready” food hot. Grilled tucker can be kept hot".

essence.evidence: It is the original guide, headings unchanged: "Follow Safe Grilling Tips".

problems.why: US spelling left in, and a slang noun dropped into an otherwise untouched sentence; representative of the whole text.
Slang word next to "refrigerator"; inconsistent and pasted-on.

problems.quote: prepared/cooked tucker or foods that will be eaten raw
problems.original: prepared/cooked foods or foods that will be eaten raw
problems.why: Mixed "tucker" and "foods" in one phrase reads awkwardly.

C.summary: The original with nouns swapped in; accurate but far too light, with US forms left and pasted-on slang.
